summary:
Alberta is a province within Canada and stands under the national framework: gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and under the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code, both added by Bill C-16 in 2017. Courts have applied those protections consistently, no Canadian jurisdiction restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities, and Canadian authorities have neither issued nor received alerts concerning trans travellers. Entry carries no trans-specific friction, and federally issued identity documents can carry an X marker.

Alberta's own statutes run against that framework. In December 2024 the legislature passed a package of three measures affecting transgender people as a class: the Education Amendment Act 2024, which requires parental opt-in for classroom instruction and sets rules on student pronouns and school sports; a health-statutes act barring puberty blockers and hormone therapy for minors; and related vital-statistics amendments. Egale Canada and the Skipping Stone Foundation announced constitutional litigation at the time, calling the package discriminatory.

The care prohibition is the element with direct bearing on a visitor. It is a statutory bar in Alberta's health statutes on puberty blockers and hormone therapy for anyone under 18, so gender-affirming medical care for a trans minor cannot be obtained in the province while it stands.

Bill 9, the Protecting Alberta's Children Statutes Amendment Act, passed at the tail of the same sitting and invoked the Charter's notwithstanding clause to shield all three laws from judicial remedy for years. Egale Canada, the Skipping Stone Foundation and five families state that their court challenge to the underlying statutes continues regardless. The laws are in force and constitutional litigation is pending.

Trans people held in federal custody inside Alberta fall under Correctional Service of Canada policy in force since 2018, which accommodates offenders on the basis of gender identity rather than sex assigned at birth. Gender-diverse offenders may request placement or transfer to a men's or women's institution aligned with their gender identity or expression, regardless of anatomy or the sex or gender marker on identity documents, and a request is refused only where the Correctional Service finds unresolvable overriding health or safety concerns. As of 2025 the service reported 90 self-identified transgender women in federal institutions, 73 housed in men's institutions and 17 in women's.

The Office of the Correctional Investigator called the 2022 gender-diversity policy an important change but flagged two gaps: no clear parameters for what counts as an overriding health or safety concern, and no dedicated mechanism for gender-diverse prisoners to report abuse.

Alberta's statutory package deliberately stops short of custody and shared facilities. Premier Danielle Smith's 12 February 2024 announcement covered the care ban, parental-consent rules for school pronouns and sexuality instruction, and a ban on trans women in women's sports, and stated that the measures would not include women's shelters, women's prisons or changing rooms. No provincial rule placing trans prisoners by birth sex was enacted, and no Alberta-specific trans-prisoner placement, special unit or segregation case is documented.
tangentialFactors:
The national hate-crime climate is deteriorating even where the statutes hold. Statistics Canada recorded 4,882 police-reported hate-crime incidents in 2024, up 1% after a 34% jump the year before. Incidents targeting sexual orientation fell 26% to 658, ending three consecutive years of increases from a 2023 peak of 889, but across the longer arc police-reported hate crime has risen for six consecutive years and is up 169% since 2018, with offences motivated by gender identity and gender expression among the fastest-growing categories. Egale Canada documents an increasingly organised anti-trans movement.

Alberta is not alone in moving against residents. Saskatchewan has enacted comparable policy rollbacks, including school-facing measures on names, pronouns and notification of parents, so the direction of provincial politics here matches a wider pattern rather than standing alone.

Other provinces run the opposite way on documents. Most allow the gender marker on official documents to be changed by declaring one's identified gender, and a 2016 amendment to one province's Vital Statistics Act removed the prior surgery requirement in favour of a declaration supported by a doctor's letter. Ontario's human rights code expressly covers gender identity and gender expression, and the Ontario Human Rights Commission publishes guidance on how such complaints are handled, which is the clearest published complaint route in the country.

Healthcare coverage is universal across Canada, so routine and emergency care carries no insurance barrier for visitors; the constraint in Alberta is the statutory prohibition on gender-affirming care for minors rather than cost or coverage.
localsOnly:
The Education Amendment Act 2024 governs school life for trans and gender-diverse students: parents must opt in to classroom instruction on gender and sexuality, staff must notify and obtain parental consent before using a student's gender-related chosen name or pronouns, and sport participation rules apply alongside it. The package also bars trans women from women's sports at the level the legislation reaches.

The health-statutes act removes puberty blockers and hormone therapy from the options available to trans minors in Alberta, and the accompanying vital-statistics amendments alter how gender is recorded in provincial registers. The precise scope of those vital-statistics changes is not set out in the sources available here.

Residents challenging the package have a live route: Egale Canada, the Skipping Stone Foundation and five families are in constitutional litigation, and the notwithstanding-clause shield in Bill 9 was enacted to keep that litigation from succeeding for years.

Provincial correctional policy on trans prisoners varies across Canada and no Alberta-specific rule is documented, so placement in a provincial facility is governed by general policy rather than a statute naming trans status. Federal prisoners inside Alberta are covered by the Correctional Service of Canada's gender-identity-based placement policy instead.

Residents have access to universal publicly funded healthcare and to discrimination complaints under the Canadian Human Rights Act, which lists gender identity and gender expression as protected grounds.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the notwithstanding-clause shield in Bill 9 carries a stated expiry date, and whether it has been renewed or extended since December 2024, is not resolved in the sources available here.

The exact wording and reach of the vital-statistics amendments passed with the December 2024 package is unresolved; the sources confirm the amendments exist but do not describe what they change for an adult resident seeking a marker change.

No Alberta-specific trans-prisoner placement, special unit or segregation case is documented, and no provincial rule placing trans prisoners by birth sex has been located. Provincial correctional policies are described only as varying.

The Office of the Correctional Investigator's criticism remains open on its own terms: what constitutes an overriding health or safety concern under the 2022 policy is undefined, and whether a reporting mechanism for gender-diverse prisoners has since been created is not sourced.

Whether Alberta-issued identity documents offer an X marker, as federal documents do, is not sourced here. Nor is the availability of any exemption, clinical-trial route or transitional provision within the ban on gender-affirming care for minors.
